item.title: Structural basis for the non-canonical nucleosome remodeling by ATRX.
item.author: Wang X, Yan S, Huang Y, Ge K, Wu Y, Xu W, Kang Y, Yao D, Liu X, Chen Y.
item.description:
Alpha-thalassemia/mental retardation syndrome X-linked (ATRX) is a sucrose nonfermentable 2 (Snf2)-family ATP-dependent chromatin remodeler essential for chromatin regulation and genome stability, but its remodeling mechanism remains unclear. Here, we report three structures of the human ATRX ATPase domain (ATRX ATPase ) in its free, nucleosome-bound, and histone-bound states, revealing a non-canonical mechanism of activity regulation and chromatin remodeling. ATRX ATPase adopts a structurally primed but autoinhibited conformation that is relieved upon nucleosome binding. ATRX favors ATP-dependent nucleosome disassembly over sliding and engages a non-canonical nucleosomal site, contacting unwrapped DNA at superhelical location (SHL) 5.5-7. item.title: Small genomes, big lessons: What viruses teach us about structure-based riboregulation.
item.author: Hann T, Jang H, Sung YC, Guh CL, Hiers NM, Tsao LH, Luo M, Pyle AM.
item.description:
RNA viruses encode multiple layers of information within a single molecule, which functions simultaneously as a template for protein synthesis and as a structured regulatory RNA. These structures control key aspects of viral gene expression, govern host interactions, and mediate immune evasion. Although the prevalence of RNA structure in viral genomes is now well established, only recently have functional and mechanistic studies begun to uncover how these elements act as regulatory modules that shape infection outcomes. With their compact genomes and experimentally tractable life cycles, RNA viruses represent powerful model systems for uncovering the fundamental building blocks of riboregulation and illuminating principles of gene control conserved across eukaryotes. item.title: How the TREX-2 complex associates with the nuclear pore.
item.author: Obarska-Kosinska A, Zhu Y, Geißler K, Rosenkranz RRE, Yokoyama N, Kreysing JP, Xing H, Glushkova D, Kubańska MA, Böhm S, Kräusslich HG, Turoňová B, Liu F, Beck M.
item.description:
Nuclear pore complexes (NPCs) control nucleocytoplasmic transport in eukaryotes, yet their architecture remains incompletely understood. Here, we report a substantially extended structure of the human NPC, obtained by combining cryo-electron tomography, crosslinking mass spectrometry, and AI-assisted integrative modeling. We resolve the molecular arrangement of translocated promoter region (TPR), NUP153, NUP50, and ZC3HC1 and reveal that five additional proteins-TMEM209, SMPD4, GANP, Centrin-2, and ENY2-are incorporated into the NPC. Unexpectedly, GANP, Centrin-2, and ENY2, core members of the TREX-2 mRNA export complex, are built into the nuclear ring. This finding establishes TREX-2 not as a transiently associated factor, but as an integral NPC module, positioning it opposite of the cytoplasmic NUP214 mRNA export platform. item.title: Amyloid-mediated RNA uptake by sperm for embryonic delivery.
item.author: Mallen WS, Zabello N, Brenner-Morton S, Sidoli S, Liang FX, Sall J, Yin J, Mathews P, Zhu M, Zhang G, Lee CL, Liao YC, Fitzpatrick AWP.
item.description:
Seminal fluid (SF) RNA is essential for embryonic development, but the mechanism by which extracellular RNA is transferred from SF to sperm remains unclear. Here, we identify a role for functional amyloid fibrils in SF that bind and traffic RNA to mammalian sperm and, upon fertilization, to the zygote. We show that highly cationic peptides in SF phase separate with RNA to form amyloid fibrils. Cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET), volume electron microscopy (volume EM), and fluorescence live-cell imaging reveal that these amyloid fibrils are internalized by mammalian sperm. Furthermore, biophysical and in vitro fertilization (IVF) experiments show that amyloid-bound RNA reaches the zygote, where molecular chaperones can control RNA dissociation from amyloid fibrils. item.title: The 9-1-1 complex protects ssDNA gaps in BRCA2-deficient cancer.
item.author: Grimsley HE, Courtemanche K, Cox S, Calder A, McDermott N, Pei X, Sharma A, Bright J, Riaz N, Setton J, Orman M, Powell SN.
item.description:
Single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) gaps are a hallmark of BRCA-deficient cells, yet the mechanisms that safeguard these lesions remain unclear. Using a genome-wide CRISPR screen in isogenic BRCA2-proficient and -deficient cancer cells, we identified the RAD9A-HUS1-RAD1 (9-1-1) complex as essential for BRCA2-deficient cell survival through an ATR-independent mechanism. In this context, loss of 9-1-1 leads to accumulation of PRIMPOL-dependent gaps that fail to undergo post-replicative repair, resulting in pathological expansion and increased DNA damage. Excessive EXO1-mediated degradation drives this genomic instability, as EXO1 depletion rescues the phenotype. We further demonstrate that the 9-1-1 complex contributes to POLζ-dependent gap filling. item.title: PARP1 directly disassembles nucleosomes to regulate DNA repair.
item.author: Verma A, Zhu C, Truong B, Bilokapic S, DeVries R, Pitre A, Bhat YA, Shelat AA, Halic M, Dao HT.
item.description:
Upon DNA damage, chromatin remodeling is rapidly initiated to promote chromatin accessibility. Although this enhanced accessibility has been linked to poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) activity, how cells overcome the nucleosome barrier remains unclear. We discovered that PARP1 directly and asymmetrically evicts histone dimers proximal to DNA strand breaks from nucleosomes to generate oriented hexasomes. In the presence of histone PARylation factor 1 (HPF1), PARP1 generates stable PARylated hexasomes that can facilitate recruitment of DNA- and PAR-dependent factors. In human cells, PARP activity directly drives chromatin accessibility and generates subnucleosomal species. Unexpectedly, we identified the C-terminal tail of histone H2A, a motif harboring recurrent cancer-associated mutations, as a critical determinant of efficient PARP1-mediated nucleosome disassembly. item.title: HP1 can act independently of H3K9 methylation to promote heterochromatin focus formation, gene repression, and organogenesis.
item.author: Delaney CE, Fol L, Gruenewald SB, You JE, Ferrario E, Moeckel MM, Stelzl L, Gasser SM, Padeken J, Mango SE.
item.description:
Histone post-translational modifications (PTMs) segregate genomes into heterochromatin and euchromatin by recruiting readers, such as Heterochromatin Protein 1, which binds methylation of histone H3 lysine 9 (H3K9me). Here, we report H3K9me-independent functions for the C. elegans HP1 orthologue HPL-2 and the H3K9 methyltransferase MET-2/SETDB1. The two colocalize in H3K9me-containing subnuclear foci independently of the PTM and each other. Their combined loss additively disrupts gene repression and organogenesis. A mutant HPL-2 deficient for H3K9me binding maintains localization to heterochromatin foci, restricts cell-fate decisions, and represses developmental genes, dependent on its multi-zinc-finger ligand, LIN-13. item.title: Protein arginine methylation promotes global 3'UTR shortening in proliferating cells.
item.author: Griffith L, Capitanchik C, Moore S, Farcas A, Gwynne M, Pedna M, Vukšinić I, Bračič V, Davey K, Jones DM, Chakrabarti AM, Lagos D, Urosevic J, Lynch JT, Ule J.
item.description:
Protein arginine methyltransferases (PRMTs) are promising anti-cancer targets, but their tumorigenic mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Here, we show that arginine methylation drives global 3'UTR shortening, thereby promoting oncogenic short isoforms. Inhibition of asymmetric dimethylation reverses this shift, with combined inhibition of asymmetric and symmetric dimethylation (DMAi) producing an even greater effect across human cancer cell lines, patient-derived organoids, and activated murine T cells, while also counteracting the shortening induced by reduced CFIm25 expression. item.title: Regulatable in vivo gene expression via adaptamers.
item.author: Bryant J, Herron L, Doctor Y, McRae F, Wang J, Hirsch T, Portell A, Kumar S, Mali P.
item.description:
Precise, reversible control of transgene expression is essential for safe and durable gene therapy, yet current inducible systems remain difficult to translate in vivo due to large size, limited induction duration, and dependence on immunogenic regulators. Here, we present the adaptamer (adenosine deaminases acting on RNA [ADAR]-modulatable aptamer), a compact ( < 120 base pair) RNA switch that couples FDA-approved small-molecule-responsive aptamers with endogenous ADAR-mediated RNA editing to regulate expression. Ligand binding stabilizes a double-stranded RNA structure that recruits ADAR to convert a stop codon into a sense codon, restoring downstream protein translation.
